front: Row picture versus column picture of $A\mathbf x=\mathbf b$
back: Row: each equation is a hyperplane, a solution lies on all. Column: $\mathbf b$ as a linear combination of the columns of $A$ with coefficients $\mathbf x$.

front: Three possible outcomes of a linear system
back: No solution, exactly one, or infinitely many. Never exactly two.
Swap two rows; scale a row by a non-zero constant; add a multiple of one row to another. They keep the solution set unchanged.
Zero rows at the bottom; each pivot (first non-zero entry) strictly to the right of the pivot above: a staircase.
Basic: unknowns in pivot columns. Free: the others; they can be chosen arbitrarily and parametrise the solution set.
Number of linearly independent columns (= rows) = number of pivots = $\dim\operatorname{Im}(A)$. Full rank: $\min(m,n)$.
$A\mathbf x=\mathbf b$ is solvable iff $\operatorname{rk}(A)=\operatorname{rk}(A|\mathbf b)$; unique iff additionally $\operatorname{rk}(A)=n$.
Particular solution $+$ any vector of $\ker(A)$. For $\mathbf b\ne\mathbf0$ the solution set is not a subspace.
$\ker A=\{\mathbf x:A\mathbf x=0\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n$; $\operatorname{Im}A=\operatorname{span}$ of the columns $\subseteq\mathbb R^m$.
Dividing by a tiny pivot gives huge multipliers that amplify rounding error; swap to the largest entry in the column. Cost of elimination $\sim n^3$.
$PA=LU$ costs $\sim n^3$ once; each new right-hand side then costs only $\sim n^2$ (two triangular solves).
$A^\top A\mathbf x=A^\top\mathbf b$, shapes $(n,n)$ and $(n,)$; residual $\mathbf b-A\mathbf x\perp$ columns of $A$. This is linear regression.
Call `np.linalg.solve(A, b)` (LU with pivoting, no explicit inverse) or `lstsq` for rectangular $A$; never `inv(A) @ b`.
